readerTitle: The quiet team and the loud team: which one should worry you?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (리모델링 업체, B2B 마케팅 에이전시, 소프트웨어 스타트업) + 실제 연구 (Jehn 1995, De Dreu & Weingart 2003, de Wit 외 2012)
insight: 좋은 팀은 갈등이 적은 팀이 아니라, 일에 대해서는 부딪히고 사람에 대해서는 부딪히지 않는 팀이다.
misconception: 조용하고 다툼 없는 팀이 건강한 팀이다. 반대로 갈등은 많을수록 좋은 아이디어가 나온다.

sources.text: Jehn, K. A. (1995). A multimethod examination of the benefits and detriments of intragroup conflict. Administrative Science Quarterly, 40(2), 256–282.
De Dreu, C. K. W., & Weingart, L. R. (2003). Task versus relationship conflict, team performance, and team member satisfaction: A meta-analysis. Journal of Applied Psychology, 88(4), 741–749.
de Wit, F. R. C., Greer, L. L., & Jehn, K. A. (2012). The paradox of intragroup conflict: A meta-analysis. Journal of Applied Psychology, 97(2), 360–390.
리모델링 업체, 에이전시, 스타트업 장면은 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: Jehn(1995)이 과업 갈등(task conflict)과 관계 갈등(relationship conflict)을 구분한 대표 연구라는 점을 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 구체 수치 없이 구분 개념만 썼습니다.
De Dreu & Weingart(2003) 메타분석은 평균적으로 과업 갈등도 성과와 부적 관계였다고 보고했습니다. de Wit 외(2012)는 과업 갈등의 효과가 조건(관계 갈등이 낮을 때, 최고경영진 팀, 비일상적 과업 등)에 따라 달라진다고 보고했습니다. 카드 5의 요약 표현이 두 논문의 결론과 맞는지 확인하세요.
카드 5의 '관계 갈등은 성과와 만족도를 일관되게 떨어뜨린다'는 표현이 두 메타분석 결과와 일치하는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: The quiet team and the loud team: which one should worry you?
body: A home renovation firm holds calm Monday meetings. Nobody pushes back. Plans get approved in ten minutes.
Across town, a B2B marketing agency runs loud meetings. People interrupt, challenge and argue for an hour.
Most owners would rather run the first team. That instinct can be wrong, and so can the opposite one.

image.label: Two meeting rooms, one silent and one noisy
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눈 일러스트. 왼쪽은 작업복 차림 리모델링 팀이 조용히 고개를 끄덕이는 회의실, 오른쪽은 에이전시 팀이 화이트보드 앞에서 손짓하며 토론하는 회의실. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which team is in more trouble?
body: You've seen one meeting from each business. You know nothing else yet.
Which team would you worry about first?

options.text: The agency. Constant arguing wears people down
options.feedback: Arguing can wear people down, but it can also catch weak ideas early. Noise alone doesn't tell you which is happening.

options.text: The renovation firm. Silence usually hides problems
options.feedback: A good suspicion, since quiet teams often bury bad news. But some teams are quiet because the work is routine and going well.

options.text: Can't tell yet. It depends on what they're arguing, or not arguing, about
options.feedback: Right. The amount of conflict matters less than its target: the work or the people. The next card shows both.

cards.title: Both teams had a conflict problem. Different ones.
body: At the renovation firm, a crew lead saw that the kitchen plan put a sink where the drain couldn't reach. He said nothing, because nobody questions the project manager. The crew tore out new cabinets two weeks later.
At the agency, a debate about a campaign slogan turned into "You always kill my ideas." Two strategists stopped talking. A client noticed they gave contradictory advice.
One team avoided useful disagreement. The other let disagreement turn personal.

cards.title: Healthy conflict
body: Researchers such as Karen Jehn separate two kinds of conflict. **Task conflict** is disagreement about the work: the plan, the facts, the best option. **Relationship conflict** is friction between people: irritation, blame, dislike.
**Healthy conflict** means plenty of the first and little of the second. The renovation crew needed more task conflict. The agency needed to stop its task conflict turning into relationship conflict.

image.label: Two arrows: one aimed at a plan, one aimed at a person
image.brief: 단순한 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 화살표는 설계도(plan)를 향하고 "Task conflict: about the work" 라벨, 녹색 계열. 오른쪽 화살표는 사람 실루엣을 향하고 "Relationship conflict: about the person" 라벨, 붉은 계열.

cards.title: One kind reliably hurts. The other depends.
body: Large reviews of team studies find relationship conflict tends to lower both performance and satisfaction.

Task conflict is mixed. A 2003 review found that, on average, it hurt performance too, mostly because work arguments easily slide into personal ones. A later 2012 review found it more often helped when relationship conflict stayed low and the decisions were complex rather than routine.
So the skill isn't encouraging conflict. It's **keeping disagreement aimed at the work**.

cards.title: Ways to argue about the work, not the person.
body: Teams with healthy conflict usually build habits like these:
list: **Agree on the goal first**, then argue about how to reach it
Describe the problem in the plan, not the person: "This drain won't reach," not "You didn't check"
Ask someone to make the strongest case for the other option
Set a decision deadline and a decider, so debates end
cards.callout: Disagreement needs a clear target and a clear finish.
cards.softwareNote: Code and design reviews are built-in task conflict. Teams that keep comments about the code ("this query will be slow") rather than the coder ("you always do this") get the benefit without the bruises.

cards.title: Task conflict has costs.
body: Even polite debate takes time. On routine work, like a standard bathroom refit, arguing over every step mostly slows the job.
It also needs trust underneath. Where people already resent each other, a challenge to an idea is heard as an attack. Fix the relationship strain before inviting more debate.
And debate without a decision rule never ends. Someone must call it, and the team must commit.

cards.title: Now it's a software startup.
body: Your engineer and marketer disagree about a new pricing page. In the meeting, the engineer says: "Marketing always wants shiny things that break." The marketer goes quiet.
What do you do?

options.text: Stop the debate and decide the pricing page yourself
options.feedback: You end the tension today, but both learn that disagreeing is unsafe. Next time they'll stay quiet, like the renovation crew.

options.text: Let them argue it out. Conflict is healthy
options.feedback: This conflict has already turned personal. Letting it run grows the relationship damage without improving the page.

options.text: Reset to the work: each states the goal, their concern and what evidence would change their mind. You decide Friday
options.feedback: You keep the useful disagreement about the page and remove the swipe at a person. A deadline stops it dragging on.

cards.title: Fight about the work, never about the people.
body: Don't judge a team by how much it argues. Judge it by what the arguments are aimed at.
**Try it today:** in your next meeting, ask one person to argue against the plan you're leaning toward. Notice whether the replies talk about the plan or the person.
